html:
In 1962 Saudi Arabia formally abolished slavery by a decree of Crown Prince Faisal. Yemen did the same that year, making them among the last countries in the world to end it in law.

Slavery in Arabia was old. Enslaved Africans arrived across the Red Sea, and some pilgrims to Mecca were tricked or sold into bondage. Enslaved people worked as servants, concubines, guards and pearl divers. Islamic law allowed slavery, and the Saudi state long resisted outside pressure.

Britain pushed for abolition for decades, and in 1936 the kingdom banned the import of new slaves. After the Second World War, criticism at the United Nations grew, and Faisal, then modernising the state, acted as part of a ten-point reform programme. The government paid owners compensation. Estimates of how many people were freed vary widely.

Compare Tunisia, which abolished slavery in 1846. Rights groups say forms of forced labour lingered under the kafala sponsorship system for migrant workers.
sum: In 1962 Saudi Arabia formally abolished slavery by a decree of Crown Prince Faisal. Yemen did the same that year, making them among the last countries in the world to end it in law.
